title: Selecting frames
summary: Measure sharpness, brightness and camera motion, then pick a subset of frames

blocks.text:
My input is 814 frames from a 34-second video circling a pumpkin on a table. I shot it in Full HD at 24 fps on a Canon EOS 600D with the 18–55 mm kit lens at 18 mm, image stabilization off. The room was dark, so exposure was set by hand: 1/125 s, f/11, ISO 3200.

In the last part of the video the camera goes down to table level, and only the lower half of the pumpkin is in view. In a full training run that section came out blurry and hazy in the trained model (notebook 06), so I only use the first 580 frames.

That's still far more than Structure-from-Motion needs: neighbouring frames are almost identical, and some are blurry where I moved the camera too fast. In this notebook I score every frame for sharpness, brightness and camera motion, and copy a subset into `work/images/`. The originals in `frames/` stay untouched.

import json, shutil, csv
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter
from tqdm.auto import tqdm

PROJECT_DIR = Path.cwd()
FRAMES_DIR = PROJECT_DIR / "frames"
WORK_DIR = PROJECT_DIR / "work"
IMAGES_DIR = WORK_DIR / "images"          # output of this notebook
WORK_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

IMAGE_EXTS = {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png"}
frame_paths = sorted(p for p in FRAMES_DIR.iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in IMAGE_EXTS)
print(f"{len(frame_paths)} frames in {FRAMES_DIR.name}/")
assert frame_paths, "No frames found — put your JPG/PNG files into frames/"

KEEP_FIRST = 580        # drop the end of the video, where the camera goes down to table level
frame_paths = frame_paths[:KEEP_FIRST]
print(f"using the first {len(frame_paths)}")

814 frames in frames/
using the first 580

## First look

All frames need the same resolution, because later I tell COLMAP they come from a single camera. Frames cut from a video carry no EXIF data, so COLMAP doesn't know the focal length. Notebook 03 estimates it from the images, and I compare that estimate with the 18 mm of the lens.

from collections import Counter
from PIL import Image

sizes = Counter(Image.open(p).size for p in frame_paths)
total_mb = sum(p.stat().st_size for p in frame_paths) / 1024**2
print("resolutions (width, height) → count:", dict(sizes))
print(f"total size: {total_mb:.0f} MB, average {total_mb / len(frame_paths) * 1024:.0f} KB per frame")

assert len(sizes) == 1, "Frames have different resolutions — they probably come from different cameras/videos."
W, H = next(iter(sizes))

resolutions (width, height) → count: {(1920, 1080): 580}
total size: 110 MB, average 195 KB per frame
16 frames spread across the video:

def show_grid(paths, titles=None, cols=4, width=16):
    rows = int(np.ceil(len(paths) / cols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(width, width / cols * rows * H / W))
    for ax in np.atleast_1d(axes).ravel():
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, p) in enumerate(zip(np.atleast_1d(axes).ravel(), paths)):
        img = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread(str(p)), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
        ax.imshow(cv2.resize(img, (W // 4, H // 4), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA))
        ax.set_title(titles[i] if titles else p.name, fontsize=9)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

overview = [frame_paths[i] for i in np.linspace(0, len(frame_paths) - 1, 16).astype(int)]
show_grid(overview)

## What makes a frame useful

| Property | Why it matters | What goes wrong otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharp** | SfM matches tiny details. Training copies whatever it sees, including blur. | Fewer matches, wrong poses, a soft or smeared model |
| **Overlap** between neighbours (≈ 70–90 %) | The same points must appear in several images to be triangulated | The reconstruction breaks into separate pieces |
| **Parallax** (the camera actually *moves*, not just rotates) | Depth is computed from the change in viewpoint | Unstable depth: many near-identical frames add cost without adding information |
| **Coverage** from all sides and heights | Every surface we want in 3D must be seen | Holes and blurry "unseen" regions |
| **Consistent exposure** | 3DGS assumes a surface has the same colour in every view | Flicker baked into the model as coloured "floaters" |
| **Static scene** | SfM and 3DGS assume nothing moves | Ghosts, wrong matches |

Coverage, exposure and a static scene are fixed once the video is recorded. Blur and spacing are things I can still control by choosing which frames to keep.

## Sharpness

I use the variance of the Laplacian, a common blur measure. The Laplacian responds to edges, blur weakens edges, so the variance drops. One frame with increasing blur:

def sharpness(gray):
    # Variance of the Laplacian, computed on a half-resolution image.
    # Downscaling first reduces the influence of sensor noise and JPEG artefacts.
    small = cv2.resize(gray, (gray.shape[1] // 2, gray.shape[0] // 2), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    return cv2.Laplacian(small, cv2.CV_64F).var()

demo = cv2.imread(str(frame_paths[len(frame_paths) // 3]), cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.5))
for ax, k in zip(axes, [0, 3, 7, 15]):
    img = demo if k == 0 else cv2.GaussianBlur(demo, (0, 0), k / 3)
    crop = img[H // 3 : H // 3 + 300, W // 3 : W // 3 + 400]
    ax.imshow(crop, cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(f"blur σ={k/3:.1f} → sharpness {sharpness(img):.1f}")
    ax.axis("off")
plt.show()

The score drops quickly with blur, but it also depends on content: wood grain scores higher than a smooth surface even when both are in focus. So instead of a fixed threshold, I compare each frame to its neighbours below.

## Brightness and motion

Brightness is the mean grey value. For motion I compute Farnebäck optical flow between consecutive frames on 480 px wide copies and take the median displacement, scaled back to full-resolution pixels. A value near zero means the camera paused.

FLOW_WIDTH = 480                      # optical flow on small images: fast, still accurate enough
flow_scale = W / FLOW_WIDTH
flow_size = (FLOW_WIDTH, round(H / flow_scale))

sharp, bright, motion = [], [], [0.0]   # motion[i] = movement from frame i-1 to i (frame 0 has none)
prev = None
for p in tqdm(frame_paths, desc="analysing frames"):
    gray = cv2.imread(str(p), cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
    sharp.append(sharpness(gray))
    bright.append(gray.mean())
    tiny = cv2.resize(gray, flow_size, interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    if prev is not None:
        flow = cv2.calcOpticalFlowFarneback(prev, tiny, None, 0.5, 3, 21, 3, 5, 1.1, 0)
        motion.append(float(np.median(np.linalg.norm(flow, axis=2))) * flow_scale)
    prev = tiny

sharp, bright, motion = map(np.array, (sharp, bright, motion))
print(f"sharpness : {sharp.min():.1f} … {sharp.max():.1f}")
print(f"brightness: {bright.min():.0f} … {bright.max():.0f}")
print(f"motion    : median {np.median(motion[1:]):.1f} px/frame, total path {motion.sum():.0f} px")

sharpness : 9.6 … 58.8
brightness: 73 … 119
motion    : median 14.0 px/frame, total path 9044 px

### Relative sharpness

Each frame's score divided by the median of the 31 frames around it. Around 1.0 means as sharp as its neighbours; a dip to 0.5 is almost always a blurry frame.

WINDOW = 31
local_median = median_filter(sharp, size=WINDOW, mode="nearest")
rel_sharp = sharp / local_median

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(15, 10), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(sharp, lw=0.8, label="sharpness")
axes[0].plot(local_median, lw=2, label=f"rolling median ({WINDOW} frames)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Laplacian var."); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].plot(rel_sharp, lw=0.8)
axes[1].axhline(1.0, c="gray", ls=":")
axes[1].set_ylabel("relative sharpness")
axes[2].plot(bright, lw=1, c="tab:orange")
axes[2].set_ylabel("brightness")
axes[3].plot(motion, lw=0.8, c="tab:green")
axes[3].set_ylabel("motion (px/frame)"); axes[3].set_xlabel("frame index")
for ax in axes: ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

What I read from these plots:

- Raw sharpness drops for the last part, from about frame 490, where the camera is low and close to the table and most of the frame is out-of-focus wood. The relative score removes this trend, and its remaining dips are individual blurry frames.
- Brightness swings smoothly as the camera moves. Exposure was fixed, so most of this is content: how much of the frame is dark table and how much is bright pumpkin. But I also had Canon's Auto Lighting Optimizer on (Standard), which adjusts brightness and contrast frame by frame. That breaks the assumption that a surface looks the same in every view, so notebook 06 learns a per-image brightness correction to absorb it.
- Several motion peaks line up with sharpness dips, which fits motion blur.
- In the low part the motion values are probably too small. Optical flow needs texture, and on the smooth, blurry table it underestimates how far the camera moved. With the full video this left the low section too sparse for matching in notebook 02, which is why the selection below has a gap rule.

### Blurriest and sharpest frames

Centre crops at full resolution, three of each:

def spread_out(order, k=3, min_gap=30):
    # Take the first k frames from `order` that are at least `min_gap` frames apart,
    # so we don't just get three consecutive frames from the same moment.
    picks = []
    for i in order:
        if all(abs(i - j) >= min_gap for j in picks):
            picks.append(int(i))
        if len(picks) == k:
            break
    return picks

order = np.argsort(rel_sharp)
picks = spread_out(order) + spread_out(order[::-1])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 8))
for ax, i in zip(axes.ravel(), picks):
    img = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread(str(frame_paths[i])), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
    ax.imshow(img[H // 2 - 200 : H // 2 + 200, W // 2 - 300 : W // 2 + 300])
    ax.set_title(f"{frame_paths[i].name}  relative sharpness {rel_sharp[i]:.2f}")
    ax.axis("off")
plt.suptitle("Top: blurriest 3   |   Bottom: sharpest 3", fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

## Selecting frames

The selection has three steps:

1. Drop frames with relative sharpness below `MIN_REL_SHARPNESS`.
2. Space frames by camera motion instead of time: split the cumulative motion into `TARGET_FRAMES` equal parts and keep the sharpest frame in each. A pause then gives one frame instead of dozens of duplicates.
3. Never leave more than `MAX_FRAME_GAP` original frames between two picks. Where a gap is larger, insert the sharpest frame from its middle and repeat.

Step 3 is the patch for the under-counted motion. `MAX_FRAME_GAP = 6` is a quarter of a second at 24 fps. With the full video it added 61 frames; on the first 580 it adds only a handful.

TARGET_FRAMES = 200         # frames picked by motion spacing (step 2)
MIN_REL_SHARPNESS = 0.8     # drop frames clearly blurrier than their neighbours (step 1)
MAX_FRAME_GAP = 6           # never skip more than this many original frames (step 3); 6 frames = 0.25 s at 24 fps

usable = rel_sharp >= MIN_REL_SHARPNESS
odometer = np.cumsum(motion)                        # distance travelled up to each frame
bins = np.linspace(0, odometer[-1], TARGET_FRAMES + 1)
bin_of_frame = np.clip(np.searchsorted(bins, odometer, side="right") - 1, 0, TARGET_FRAMES - 1)

selected = []
for b in range(TARGET_FRAMES):
    candidates = np.where((bin_of_frame == b) & usable)[0]
    if len(candidates):
        selected.append(int(candidates[np.argmax(rel_sharp[candidates])]))
motion_picks = np.array(sorted(set(selected)))

def fill_gaps(picks, max_gap):
    # Insert the sharpest usable frame from the middle of every gap that is too big,
    # and repeat until no gap exceeds max_gap.
    picks = list(picks)
    while True:
        filled, added = [picks[0]], False
        for a, b in zip(picks, picks[1:]):
            if b - a > max_gap:
                mid = (a + b) // 2
                window = range(max(a + 1, mid - max_gap // 2), min(b - 1, mid + max_gap // 2) + 1)
                candidates = [i for i in window if usable[i]] or list(window)
                filled.append(max(candidates, key=lambda i: rel_sharp[i]))
                added = True
            filled.append(b)
        picks = filled
        if not added:
            return np.array(picks)

selected = fill_gaps(motion_picks, MAX_FRAME_GAP)
gap_filled = np.setdiff1d(selected, motion_picks)

print(f"blurry frames rejected   : {(~usable).sum()} of {len(frame_paths)}")
print(f"picked by motion spacing : {len(motion_picks)}  (target {TARGET_FRAMES})")
print(f"added to fill gaps       : {len(gap_filled)}")
print(f"frames selected in total : {len(selected)}")

blurry frames rejected   : 53 of 580
picked by motion spacing : 182  (target 200)
added to fill gaps       : 12
frames selected in total : 194

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(15, 6), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(rel_sharp, lw=0.7, c="gray", label="relative sharpness")
axes[0].scatter(np.where(~usable)[0], rel_sharp[~usable], c="red", s=12, label="rejected (blurry)", zorder=3)
axes[0].scatter(motion_picks, rel_sharp[motion_picks], c="tab:blue", s=12, label="selected (motion spacing)", zorder=3)
axes[0].scatter(gap_filled, rel_sharp[gap_filled], c="tab:purple", s=12, label="selected (gap filling)", zorder=3)
axes[0].axhline(MIN_REL_SHARPNESS, c="red", ls=":")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right"); axes[0].set_ylabel("relative sharpness")

axes[1].plot(odometer, c="tab:green", lw=1.2, label="camera odometer (cumulative motion)")
axes[1].scatter(motion_picks, odometer[motion_picks], c="tab:blue", s=10, label="motion spacing", zorder=3)
axes[1].scatter(gap_filled, odometer[gap_filled], c="tab:purple", s=10, label="gap filling", zorder=3)
axes[1].legend(loc="upper left"); axes[1].set_ylabel("pixels moved"); axes[1].set_xlabel("frame index")
for ax in axes: ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

In the lower plot the blue picks are evenly spaced in height (motion), not in frame index. Where the curve is flat, the purple gap-filling picks take over. Motion spacing gave fewer than 200 frames, because some motion bins contained only blurry frames.

### Overlap

The image shift between two consecutive picks is roughly the camera motion between them. I used 30 % of the image width as a rough upper limit for reliable matching.

gaps = odometer[selected[1:]] - odometer[selected[:-1]]
gap_pct = gaps / W * 100
print(f"shift between consecutive selected frames: median {np.median(gap_pct):.1f} %, "
      f"max {gap_pct.max():.1f} % of image width")
print(f"largest gap in original frames: {np.diff(selected).max()} (limit {MAX_FRAME_GAP})")

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 2.5))
plt.bar(range(len(gap_pct)), gap_pct, color=np.where(gap_pct > 30, "red", "tab:blue"))
plt.axhline(30, c="red", ls=":")
plt.ylabel("% of width"); plt.xlabel("selected frame pair"); plt.title("Image shift between consecutive selected frames")
plt.show()

big = np.where(gap_pct > 30)[0]
if len(big):
    print("shift above 30 % after:", [frame_paths[selected[i]].name for i in big],
          "-> raise TARGET_FRAMES or lower MIN_REL_SHARPNESS")
else:
    print("no shift above 30 %")

shift between consecutive selected frames: median 2.3 %, max 10.8 % of image width
largest gap in original frames: 6 (limit 6)
no shift above 30 %
Nothing is written to disk until the next section, so the three parameters can be changed and the cells above re-run.

## Writing the selection

The frames are copied byte for byte, since re-saving would compress the JPEGs a second time. They keep full resolution; notebook 06 makes its own smaller copies for training. The scores go to `work/frame_metrics.csv` and the parameters to `work/frame_selection.json`. `work/images/` is cleared first, so re-running gives a clean result.

selected_set = set(selected.tolist())

if IMAGES_DIR.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(IMAGES_DIR)
IMAGES_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)

for i in tqdm(selected, desc="copying"):
    shutil.copy2(frame_paths[i], IMAGES_DIR / frame_paths[i].name)

with open(WORK_DIR / "frame_metrics.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["frame", "sharpness", "relative_sharpness", "brightness", "motion_px", "selected"])
    for i, p in enumerate(frame_paths):
        w.writerow([p.name, f"{sharp[i]:.3f}", f"{rel_sharp[i]:.3f}", f"{bright[i]:.2f}",
                    f"{motion[i]:.2f}", int(i in selected_set)])

(WORK_DIR / "frame_selection.json").write_text(json.dumps({
    "target_frames": TARGET_FRAMES,
    "min_rel_sharpness": MIN_REL_SHARPNESS,
    "max_frame_gap": MAX_FRAME_GAP,
    "num_input_frames": len(frame_paths),
    "num_selected": int(len(selected)),
    "image_size": [W, H],
    "selected": [frame_paths[i].name for i in selected],
}, indent=2))

n_written = len(list(IMAGES_DIR.iterdir()))
print(f"{n_written} images written to {IMAGES_DIR.relative_to(PROJECT_DIR)}/")
194 images written to work/images/

## Result

194 of the first 580 frames are in `work/images/`: 53 were rejected as blurry, 182 picked by motion spacing and 12 added to fill gaps. Two things matter later:

- There's no EXIF, so notebook 03 estimates the focal length from the images.
- The file names keep the original frame numbers, so sorted order is time order. Notebook 02 relies on that for sequential matching.
